output.query: late-onset migraine aura after age 50 aphasic aura versus transient ischaemic attack

results.finding: Speech and/or language disturbance is a typical aura symptom; aphasia is regarded as a unilateral symptom. Typical aura symptoms spread gradually over 5 minutes or more and each lasts 5-60 minutes.
results.source: Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society. ICHD-3. Cephalalgia 2018;38:1-211

results.finding: Migrainous accompaniments can begin after age 50, often without a prior headache history; features that favour them over TIA include gradual build-up and march of symptoms, serial progression from one modality to another, and repeated identical episodes.
results.source: Fisher CM. Late-life migraine accompaniments as a cause of unexplained transient ischemic attacks. Can J Neurol Sci 1980;7:9-17

results.finding: Late-life migraine accompaniments are a diagnosis of exclusion; neuroimaging and vascular investigation are needed to exclude ischaemia, and positive symptoms with gradual spread favour aura over TIA.
results.source: Vongvaivanich K, Lertakyamanee P, Silberstein SD, Dodick DW. Late-life migraine accompaniments: a narrative review. Cephalalgia 2015;35:894-911

output.summary: Aura can begin after 50; it is distinguished from TIA by gradual spread and repeated identical episodes, and only after imaging and vascular studies exclude ischaemia.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Three stereotyped expressive dysphasia episodes building over 5-8 min, lasting 15-25 min, each followed by headache; 4 of 6 C characteristics; onset after 50 and isolated aphasic aura flagged; no GCA symptoms; normal examination
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache and aura history with examination and SNNOOP10 red-flag review, applying each ICHD-3 1.2 criterion
action_criteria.rationale: The history carries the diagnosis (gradual build-up, duration, headache after every episode, stereotyped recurrence) and identifies the red flags (first aura after 50, isolated aphasic aura) that make imaging and a GCA screen necessary before criterion D can be accepted.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No acute or old infarct, haemorrhage, mass, white matter disease or superficial siderosis
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI with DWI for a first aura after age 50 presenting as isolated aphasia
action_criteria.rationale: A first aura after 50 and an isolated aphasic aura are red flags for a secondary cause (AHS neuroimaging evidence assessment, Evans RW et al., Headache 2020;60:318-336). MRI with DWI and SWI excludes infarction, a structural lesion and amyloid-related haemorrhage; a normal DWI excludes infarction, not TIA, which remains a clinical judgement.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No intracranial or cervical arterial stenosis, occlusion or dissection
action_criteria.label: MR angiography of the head and neck for recurrent transient aphasia at 52
action_criteria.rationale: Recurrent stereotyped focal episodes in a 52-year-old with hypercholesterolaemia raise large-artery disease (for example left carotid or MCA stenosis); vessel imaging is part of excluding ischaemia. Recommended rather than required because the clinical features are those of aura.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: ESR 12 mm/h and CRP 2 mg/L (normal); HbA1c 37 mmol/mol; LDL 2.4 mmol/L on atorvastatin
action_criteria.label: ESR and CRP to screen for giant cell arteritis at 52, with glucose, HbA1c and lipids for her vascular risk review
action_criteria.rationale: New headache after 50 calls for an inflammatory-marker screen for giant cell arteritis; the metabolic and lipid values inform the statin review. Recommended: GCA is clinically unlikely (no jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual loss).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interaction with her medicines; cardiovascular evaluation advised before a first triptan given her risk factors
action_criteria.label: Check a triptan against her aspirin, atorvastatin and paracetamol
action_criteria.rationale: Optional: no interaction changes management; the triptan label caution about cardiovascular risk factors is part of the acute-treatment must.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on late-life migraine accompaniments and the features separating aura from TIA
action_criteria.label: Literature on late-onset migraine aura and its distinction from TIA
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; not a clinical step in the patient's pathway.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for presumed TIA: the episodes have the features of migraine aura (gradual build-up over minutes, previous identical attacks, migrainous headache after each) and imaging shows no infarct.
required_recommendations: Explain the diagnosis: migraine with aphasic (typical) aura, ICHD-3 1.2.1, beginning at 52; the gradual build-up, headache after every episode and normal imaging distinguish it from TIA.
Stop aspirin: it was started for presumed TIA, the episodes have the features of aura and imaging shows no infarct or arterial disease, and she has no other indication for antiplatelet therapy.
Review atorvastatin against her own 10-year cardiovascular risk (QRISK3 with her lipid profile and blood pressure), not against the TIA label.

Acute treatment at headache onset: ibuprofen 400 mg or naproxen 500 mg with an antiemetic; a triptan is an option at headache onset after a cardiovascular evaluation, which the label advises in triptan-naive patients with several risk factors.
Keep a headache diary; prevention is not indicated at three attacks in four months; review if attacks become more frequent or the aura changes.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here

accepted: Migraine with aphasic aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) — late-onset de novo aura in a postmenopausal woman after TIA exclusion

differential.diagnosis: Transient ischaemic attack (left carotid or MCA territory)
differential.key_features: Build-up over 5-8 minutes, three identical episodes each followed by migrainous headache, and full recovery favour aura; MRI shows no infarct and MRA no arterial stenosis. Normal DWI excludes infarction, not TIA; the distinction is clinical.

differential.diagnosis: Focal seizure with speech arrest or dysphasia
differential.key_features: Awareness preserved, no automatisms, 15-25 minute duration and a migrainous headache after every episode argue against it; normal MRI.
No jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual loss or polymyalgic symptoms; ESR 12 mm/h and CRP 2 mg/L.

differential.diagnosis: Transient focal neurological episodes of cerebral amyloid angiopathy
differential.key_features: Age 52 is young for CAA and the episodes are followed by migrainous headache; SWI shows no microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis.
The episodes are language-specific with preserved memory and awareness, not amnestic.
No family history of stroke or dementia and no white matter disease on MRI.

key_clinical_evidence: A first aura after 50 and an isolated aphasic aura are red flags: brain MRI is required, with vessel imaging and an ESR/CRP screen, before migraine with aura is accepted.
Aphasia is a typical aura symptom and counts as unilateral (ICHD-3); with gradual spread, 15-25 minute duration and headache within 60 minutes the attacks meet 4 of 6 C characteristics.
Normal DWI excludes infarction, not TIA; aura is distinguished from TIA clinically (gradual build-up, repeated identical episodes, headache after each).
Aspirin started for presumed TIA should be stopped once the episodes are recognised as aura; the statin is reviewed by her own cardiovascular risk.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The episodes build up over 5-8 minutes, recur identically and are followed by migrainous headache each time; with normal MRI and MRA they are aphasic aura. The TIA work-up is appropriate at her age, but its normal result points to migraine.
red_herrings.data_point: New aphasic episodes at 52 referred as TIA
red_herrings.intended_effect: May anchor on TIA and lead to antithrombotic therapy

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Modest risk factors raise the prior for TIA but do not override the aura features; MRA shows no large-artery disease.
red_herrings.data_point: Hypercholesterolaemia and borderline blood pressure in a postmenopausal woman
red_herrings.intended_effect: Vascular risk factors make TIA seem the obvious explanation

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The aspirin was started empirically before specialist assessment; it is not evidence for TIA and should be stopped once aura is recognised.
red_herrings.data_point: Aspirin started by the GP after the second episode
red_herrings.intended_effect: May be read as confirmation that the episodes are TIAs

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Migraine aura can begin after 50 (late-life migraine accompaniments); it is accepted only after imaging and vascular studies are normal. The earlier brief coloured visual phenomena may have been unrecognised visual auras.
red_herrings.data_point: First aura at 52 without a personal history of migraine
red_herrings.intended_effect: Aura is usually a diagnosis of younger adults, so late onset suggests a secondary cause

sequence_constraints.reason: The structured history identifies the red flags (first aura after 50, isolated aphasic aura) that make imaging necessary.

findings.result: Three stereotyped episodes in 4 months, first at 52. No personal history of migraine; a few brief episodes of coloured visual phenomena lasting minutes 5-10 years ago, never assessed.
Speech and language only: word-finding difficulty with circumlocution and effortful, broken phrases (expressive dysphasia), awareness preserved. No visual, sensory, motor or brainstem symptoms.
Builds up over 5-8 min, peaks at 10-15 min and clears over 5-8 min; total 15-25 min; full recovery each time.
Follows every episode within 10-30 min: left-sided, throbbing, 7/10, with photophobia and nausea, lasting 8-12 h.
No jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual loss, fever, weight loss or polymyalgic symptoms.
Normal language (fluency, repetition, comprehension, naming) and normal neurological examination; no carotid bruit; BP 134/82 mmHg, regular pulse 72.

Onset of aura after age 50: present. New headache pattern: present. Isolated aphasic aura: present. Systemic symptoms, neoplasm history, deficit outside the episodes, thunderclap onset, positional or Valsalva features, papilloedema, painful eye, trauma and medication overuse: absent.
Aspirin 75 mg started by the GP after the second episode for a TIA query; atorvastatin 20 mg started after the first; paracetamol for the headaches. No hormonal therapy.

clinical_assessment.impression: 1. Three attacks fulfilling ICHD-3 1.2 criteria A-C (4 of 6 C characteristics; aphasia counts as unilateral): the clinical features are those of migraine with typical (aphasic) aura, ICHD-3 1.2.1. 2. Red flags present: first aura after age 50, isolated aphasic aura; criterion D depends on excluding ischaemic and structural causes. 3. No clinical features of giant cell arteritis. Normal examination.

scores.ICHD-3 1.2 criterion C characteristics m: 4 of 6 (spread, 5-60 min duration, unilateral, headache within 60 min; no positive symptom, no succession)
scores.SNNOOP10 flags present: 3 (onset after 50, new pattern, isolated aphasic aura)

alternatives: Ibuprofen 400 mg or naproxen 500 mg with an antiemetic at headache onset
contraindications: Sumatriptan (SmPC): ischaemic heart disease, previous stroke or TIA, peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, hemiplegic migraine and migraine with brainstem aura.
interactions: Sumatriptan with atorvastatin, aspirin or paracetamol: no clinically significant interaction.
Aspirin with ibuprofen or naproxen: additive gastrointestinal bleeding risk; regular ibuprofen taken before aspirin can blunt its antiplatelet effect.
sumatriptan.proposed: sumatriptan for acute treatment, against current aspirin 75 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily and paracetamol as needed
sumatriptan.summary: No interaction of sumatriptan with her current medicines; label advises cardiovascular evaluation before a first triptan when several risk factors are present. Sources: sumatriptan SmPC; BNF.
warnings: Triptan-naive patients with several cardiovascular risk factors (for example postmenopausal age, hypercholesterolaemia, raised blood pressure, overweight) should have a cardiovascular evaluation before the first dose (label).
Triptans are taken at headache onset; a dose during the aura is ineffective.
Low-dose aspirin increases bleeding risk; continued use needs an indication.
Acute medication on 10 or more days a month (triptans) or 15 or more days (paracetamol, NSAIDs) risks medication-overuse headache.

additional_observations: Indication: recurrent transient expressive dysphasia at 52, TIA query.
Technique: sagittal T1, axial T2, FLAIR, DWI with ADC and SWI.
Ventricles and sulci normal for age. No microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis.

findings.location: whole brain including both perisylvian regions and the posterior fossa

signal_characteristics.FLAIR: no cortical or white matter signal change

mri.impression: Normal MRI brain. No acute or old infarct, haemorrhage, mass, white matter lesion or superficial siderosis.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: expressive aphasia at 52 with vascular risk factors looks exactly like TIA; key distinguishing features are gradual onset and subsequent headache; prior incomplete visual aura history overlooked
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Diagnostic puzzle: late-onset aphasic aura needs MRI, vessel imaging and a GCA screen before migraine is accepted, and the empirical aspirin and statin need review

patient.history_present_illness:
A 52-year-old British woman was urgently referred to the neurology outpatient clinic after three episodes over the past 4 months of transient expressive language difficulty. Each episode has a similar character: over a few minutes she becomes unable to find words she knows, using substituted or circumlocutory language ('the thing you use to write with' instead of 'pen'), and those around her notice she is speaking in broken, effortful phrases. She remains fully conscious and aware during the episode and is frustrated by her inability to express herself. The episodes develop gradually over approximately 5-8 minutes, peak in severity around 10-15 minutes, then resolve over another 5-8 minutes — total duration 15-25 minutes. Each episode has been followed within 10-30 minutes by a left-sided throbbing headache, photophobia, and nausea rated 7/10 lasting 8-12 hours.

Her GP immediately referred her for urgent TIA assessment given the language symptoms and her age. She has mildly elevated cholesterol (on atorvastatin 20 mg started after the first episode by her GP). Her blood pressure has been borderline (lifestyle advice only, no treatment); she has no AF, no diabetes, and no prior stroke. She is a non-smoker. She is post-menopausal (stopped periods age 51). She is not on any hormonal therapy. Her husband has severe migraines with visual aura. She has no prior personal history of migraine. On very careful questioning during the neurology consultation, she recalls that approximately 5-10 years ago she occasionally had brief episodes of 'colours in her vision' for a few minutes that she dismissed — she never told anyone.
